plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked 6 × 6 cross-reaction matrix from Karl Landsteiner's 14 November 1901 Vienna paper ('Über Agglutinationserscheinungen normalen menschlichen Blutes') tests the sera and red cells of six healthy lab colleagues (Dr St., Dr Plecnik, Dr Sturl, Dr Erdheim, Zaritsch, and Landsteiner), sorting human blood into Group A, Group B, and Group C (O).

teach_overlay.label: 14 NOV 1901 · 6 × 6 AGGLUTINATION TABLE (GROUPS A, B, AND C/O)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked 6 × 6 agglutination table on period paper from Landsteiner's 14 November 1901 paper showing smooth mixing (–) vs fatal clumping (+) across Groups A, B, and C (O)
teach_overlay.scale: a single mismatched transfusion can clump and shatter billions of red blood cells inside a patient's veins in minutes
teach_overlay.who_card: Karl Landsteiner (1868–1943) — Austrian pathologist and immunologist

plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period parchment, an inked coagulation and scale comparison contrasts untreated drawn blood clotting solid in glass in 4–6 minutes against blood mixed with 0.2% sodium citrate (2 g per litre, less than half a teaspoon) staying liquid in cold storage for 2–3 weeks, enabling 118.5 million donations/year.

teach_overlay.label: 4–6 MIN CLOT VS 2–3 WEEKS LIQUID (0.2% SODIUM CITRATE)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked coagulation & scale chart comparing 4–6 minutes (untreated blood clotting in glass) vs 2–3 weeks (with 0.2% sodium citrate in cold storage) and 118.5 million safe blood donations per year today
teach_overlay.scale: just two grammes of sodium citrate per litre of blood — less than half a teaspoon — turned a 6-minute surgical emergency into modern blood banks
teach_overlay.timeline_step: 4/6 · 23 Jan 1915 & Nov 1917 (Lewisohn's 0.2% sodium citrate & WWI blood bank)
